## Before the Rail

Railways are one of the few technologies whose basic idea predates the machinery that made them famous. A rail is a track that guides a wheel, and the principle of guiding a load along a fixed path is very old. Ropes, slipways, and rollers were in use long before anyone thought to fix a flat or grooved surface under a cart so that its wheels would stay on it. The story of the railway is therefore less a story of a single invention than of a long accumulation of small improvements, each of which made it cheaper to move heavy things over land, until the moment when a steam engine could be put on the track and do the work of many horses.

The most famous early example of a guided way is the diolkos, a paved trackway that crossed the Isthmus of Corinth in Greece. It is generally dated to around 600 BC, and it was used to haul ships overland on wheeled wooden cradles, saving the long sea voyage around the Peloponnese. Its surface was cut with two parallel grooves, which kept the cradles aligned. Whether ships were moved quickly or slowly is uncertain, and the road was probably used as much for smaller vessels and cargo as for warships, but the diolkos demonstrates a principle the railway would later rely on: a load moved more efficiently when the ground beneath it was prepared to receive it.

Roman roads carried wheeled traffic across Europe for centuries, but they were built for general use and not for the particular economics of heavy freight. The real pressure toward the railway came from the mines of late medieval and early modern Europe. As mines went deeper, the cost of hauling ore, rock, and water out of the ground rose steeply. Men and animals could carry only so much, and the ways between a pit and the nearest river or road were often rough. Miners learned that a cart running on a smooth, fixed surface needed far less force to move than the same cart rolling over mud and stones. The advantage was not subtle. A horse pulling a laden wagon on a level timber track could haul several times the weight it could manage on an ordinary road, and the timber was cheap, especially in places where forests were close at hand.

The modern historian has to be careful not to read the railway's later success back into these early uses. Most of the wooden ways of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries were short, local, and private. They connected a pit to a wharf or a works, and they were often dismantled when the seam was exhausted. Nobody thought of them as a network, let alone a public system. Yet they established the core of the idea: a fixed route, a vehicle designed to run on it, and a motive force that was sized to the load. Everything that followed, from the cast-iron rail to the steam locomotive to the timetable, was a refinement of that bargain between the wheel and the track.

## Wooden Roads Under the Ground

The clearest picture of the early mine railway comes from Georg Agricola, the German scholar whose book *De re metallica*, published in 1556, gathered and illustrated the practices of the metal-mining industry. Agricola's woodcuts show carts running on timber rails inside and outside the workings, with the carts pushed by men or pulled by horses. The text describes the carts as made to fit the rails, with flanged wheels or with guides on the rails themselves. Agricola was writing about what he had seen in the mining districts of central Europe, and his account suggests that the wooden way was already a familiar tool by the middle of the sixteenth century.

The problem with wood was that it wore out quickly under heavy loads, and that the wheels of the carts wore the rails as much as the rails wore the wheels. Several solutions emerged, and they map roughly onto the early history of the railway's materials. In some places the wooden rail was capped with a strip of iron, which reduced wear and extended the life of the track. In others, the timber was replaced entirely with iron as the metal became cheaper and more plentiful. The iron-capped wooden rail was an intermediate stage, and it is a useful example of how engineers in this period tended to make incremental changes instead of sweeping ones. A new material was introduced where it solved the most pressing problem, and the rest of the system was left alone until it too became the limit.

The coal districts of north-east England provided the greatest concentration of early wagonways. Coal was heavy and bulky, and the mines of the Tyne and Wear valleys sat inland, a considerable distance from the staiths, or loading wharves, on the rivers where the coal could be shipped to London and to the coastal towns. From the late seventeenth century onward, the region developed a dense web of wooden wagonways connecting pits to the riverside. Horses drew trains of wagons along these tracks, and the trains were sometimes linked together in long strings. The wagonways were usually owned by the mine owners or by consortia of them, and they were used for coal alone. The coal owners carefully controlled the access to these routes, which gave the wagonways a commercial and political significance far beyond their modest length.

The Tyneside wagonways had their own culture. The horsemen who drove the trains were a recognisable working group, and the routes became the subject of disputes over right of way, rates, and the access of independent carriers. Some of the wagonways carried passengers informally, and the boundary between a freight line and a public conveyance was never sharp. A later generation of historians has emphasised that these lines were not simply primitive forerunners of the railway. They were a commercial system, shaped by the economics of coal and by the bargaining power of the owners who controlled them. The railway that eventually emerged would inherit both the engineering and the commercial habits of these early ways.

## Iron Rails and the Horse

The transition from timber to iron rail is usually associated with the Shropshire ironworks of the Darby family at Coalbrookdale. Abraham Darby III was a leading figure in the Coalbrookdale company, which was famous for cast iron, and in 1767 it laid cast-iron rails for a tramway serving its own works. The rails were short, flanged plates, cast in lengths that were bolted together. Iron was far more durable than oak, and it could be cast into shapes that resisted the wear of the wheels better. The Coalbrookdale experiment was not the first use of iron on a wagonway, but it was the most influential, and it showed that iron could be produced in quantities and at prices that made it sensible for a railway rather than a special luxury.

Cast-iron rails had their own weaknesses. Cast iron is brittle, and the early rails were prone to fracture under the impact of heavy wheels and irregular ground. Engineers responded with a variety of designs. The plateway, in which the wheels ran on flat plates and were guided by flanges on the wheels themselves, was common in the early ironworks districts. The edge rail, in which the wheels ran on the top of a rail and were guided by the rail's shape, was developed later and eventually became the standard. Benjamin Outram, whose name appears on the word "outram" for the early tramroad, and who worked on the Little Eaton gangway in Derbyshire in the 1790s, was among the engineers who helped to make the iron tramroad a practical instrument. The variety of designs in this period reflects a field with no settled consensus, and the railway's eventual standards emerged from the competition among these experiments.

The horse remained the principal motive power on most of these lines for decades, and it is easy to underestimate how much the horse could do. A single horse on a level iron track could pull a train of wagons with a combined weight of several tons, and the efficiency of the arrangement was a substantial improvement on road carriage. The horse was also flexible. It could work on a short branch, and it could be turned to other tasks when the line was idle. The limitation was that the horse was expensive to feed and house, and that its strength was limited. On steep grades, the horse was of little use, and inclined planes were often worked by fixed engines hauling the wagons up and down with ropes.

The horse railway reached a kind of public recognition with the Surrey Iron Railway, which opened in 1803 and is often described as the first public railway in the world. It was a horse-drawn tramway connecting Wandsworth with Croydon, and it was authorised by an Act of Parliament that allowed it to carry goods for any carrier willing to pay the tolls, not just for its owners. This principle, known as common carriage, was important. It meant the railway was a public highway in a legal sense, open to traffic from many operators, and not simply a private conveyance for one owner's goods. The Surrey line and a handful of similar schemes established the legal template that many later railways would follow, and their survival into the steam age is a reminder of how much the early railway depended on the framework of Parliament and property.

## The Steam Engine Finds Its Road

The steam engine that made the railway possible had its own long development. Thomas Newcomen's atmospheric engine, built in the first decade of the eighteenth century and widely used for pumping water from mines, used a piston moved by the condensation of steam in a cylinder. It was inefficient, consuming large quantities of fuel, but it was reliable, and it solved a problem that mines could not avoid. James Watt, a Glasgow instrument maker who worked on a model of Newcomen's engine, saw that the condensation of steam in the working cylinder wasted heat, and that a separate condenser would greatly improve the engine's economy. His patent of 1769 and his partnership with Matthew Boulton in the Soho works at Birmingham produced the more efficient engines that would power the early factories and mills.

Watt's engines were built primarily as stationary machines, turning wheels in textile mills and pumping water from mines. They were heavy, and their boilers were limited in pressure by the materials and the knowledge of the time. Watt himself was reluctant to build high-pressure engines, fearing that they would be dangerous, and he thought that the most useful applications would be in the fixed installations his firm supplied. The fact that the first successful locomotives used high-pressure steam, and that these steam engines were compact enough to fit on a carriage, owed something to other engineers who were willing to take the risk.

The first attempts to put steam engines on wheels were made on roads, not rails. Nicolas-Joseph Cugnot built a steam carriage for the French army in the late 1760s, and his machine, which was intended to haul artillery, ran at walking pace and was famously difficult to steer. The road engine was a dead end for practical purposes because roads were uneven, and the engines of the period were too heavy and too unreliable for the job. Several British engineers, including William Murdoch and Richard Trevithick, experimented with road steam carriages around the turn of the nineteenth century. Trevithick's road carriage of 1801 ran in Cornwall and carried passengers, but it was abandoned when the roads proved unsuitable and the engine's boiler gave trouble.

The move to rails solved part of this problem. A rail gave the engine a surface on which the wheels could grip and a path that could be kept clear. It also reduced the rolling resistance of the carriage, and this made the steam engine's modest power sufficient for useful loads. The step from road to rail was therefore not a matter of engineering novelty alone. It was a shift in the physics of the problem, one that the earlier mine railways had already prepared.

## Trevithick, Blenkinsop and the First Locomotives

Richard Trevithick made the first recorded run of a steam locomotive on rails in February 1804, at the Penydarren ironworks near Merthyr Tydfil in south Wales. The engine was a high-pressure machine built to haul iron from the works to the canal, and on the day of its trial it pulled a train of five wagons carrying about ten tons of iron, together with around seventy men riding on the loads, over a tramroad of roughly nine miles. The engine was heavy for the cast-iron rails of the period, and the rails were broken by its weight, so the experiment did not lead to a continuing service. Trevithick himself did not pursue the locomotive commercially. He moved on to other projects, including a steam dredger and mining engines, and he died in relative poverty in 1833.

The Penydarren trial was important as a proof of concept. It showed that a steam engine could move a useful load on a plateway, and it drew the attention of other engineers to the possibility of mechanical haulage. Among those engineers was John Blenkinsop, the manager of the Middleton colliery near Leeds. Blenkinsop worried that a smooth-wheeled locomotive would slip on the rails and fail to grip, and he proposed a rack-and-pinion system in which the locomotive's driving wheel engaged with a toothed rail alongside the track. Matthew Murray, an engineer at the Round Foundry in Leeds, built the engine that tested the system. The locomotive, called *Salamanca*, went into service on the Middleton Railway in 1812, and it is generally regarded as the first commercially successful steam locomotive.

Blenkinsop's rack system was a clever response to a real problem, but it was not the solution that prevailed. The contrast between the rack and the smooth-wheel locomotive became one of the central arguments of the early steam railway. The rack was expensive to construct, and it was ultimately unnecessary, because the adhesion between a smooth wheel and a smooth rail proved to be sufficient for most purposes. Several engineers demonstrated this, and they made it possible for the locomotive to run on ordinary rails. The rack survived in mountain railways, where its grip on steep gradients remained valuable, but for the level or gently graded lines of the industrial districts the friction of the wheel on the rail was enough.

The engines that followed the Middleton locomotive were built by a generation of engineers in the north-east of England. William Hedley's *Puffing Billy*, built for the Wylam colliery near Newcastle around 1813 or 1814, used smooth wheels and demonstrated that adhesion alone would serve. George Stephenson, a colliery engineer who had worked on the pumping engines of Killingworth, built a series of locomotives for the same district, the best known of them being *Blücher*, completed in 1814 and later rebuilt. Stephenson was a self-taught engineer who combined a practical mechanic's skill with a willingness to learn from the designs of others, and his engines were improved in a series of incremental steps that made them more reliable and more powerful. He would become the figure most closely associated with the early railway, though the foundation of his work lay in the experiments of others.

## Stephenson, Stockton and the First Public Lines

The Stockton and Darlington Railway, authorised by Parliament in 1821, is conventionally regarded as the first public railway that used steam locomotives for the bulk of its traffic. Its promoters were mostly Quaker businessmen from Darlington, and their principal aim was to carry coal from the inland collieries of County Durham to the port of Stockton on the Tees, from which it could be shipped. The line was originally designed for horse traction, but George Stephenson persuaded the promoters that locomotives would be cheaper and more effective. The company hired him as engineer, and in September 1825 the railway opened with a locomotive called *Locomotion No. 1*, which hauled a train of coal wagons and a number of passenger carriages.

The opening of the Stockton and Darlington was a notable occasion, and contemporary accounts record crowds gathering along the route and passengers riding in the carriages. The line did not yet operate as a fully integrated passenger railway. Passenger traffic was carried in a mixture of vehicles, and the company did not yet have a settled schedule. But the Stockton and Darlington showed that steam locomotives could work a public line for public purposes, and it established a model that was widely copied: a company incorporated by Act of Parliament, a line built to a specified route, and a mix of freight and passenger services. The railway also proved that a locomotive could make money, which was the question investors cared most about.

The Stockton and Darlington's influence depended in part on the fact that its engineer was about to become the most famous railway engineer in Britain. Stephenson's career took a decisive turn in the years after the line opened, and his engines and his surveying skill were in demand across the north of England. His son Robert, who would later build important railways of his own, worked with him on the early lines, and the Stephensons became a family firm with an international reputation. The company at Newcastle that built their locomotives produced engines for railways in many countries in the following decades, and the locomotive shops became a model for industrial production. The success of the Stockton and Darlington was in this sense as much a matter of organisation and reputation as of machinery.

The early railways were shaped by the regional economies they served. Coal, lime, stone, and iron were the cargoes that made the first lines pay, and the routes followed the paths of the industries that needed them. Passenger traffic was often an afterthought, and in many cases the owners did not expect it to be profitable. The railway was a freight carrier first and a passenger carrier second, and the railway companies would struggle for decades to reconcile these two purposes. The Stockton and Darlington was a coal railway with a passenger addition, and that pattern would repeat across the country as the network grew.

## Liverpool, Manchester and the Idea of the Timetable

The Liverpool and Manchester Railway, which opened on 15 September 1830, is often described as the first modern railway, and the description has some justification. It was a double-track line between two major commercial centres, built to carry passengers and freight in quantity, and it was operated by locomotives on a regular timetable. The railway was promoted by Liverpool merchants who wanted a faster link to the cotton manufacturers of Manchester, and it was designed by George Stephenson and his team. The line crossed Chat Moss, a large peat bog, which was a considerable engineering challenge, and it required deep cuttings and embankments through difficult country.

The opening day of the Liverpool and Manchester is one of the most celebrated events in railway history, and it was marked by tragedy. The Prime Minister's colleague William Huskisson, who was a Member of Parliament and had been involved with the railway's promotion, was struck by the locomotive *Rocket* as he stepped down from a carriage at Parkside. He died from his injuries later that day. The accident was a sobering reminder of the dangers of the new machinery, and it made the public aware that the railway would create new risks as well as new opportunities. It also established the principle that railways would be watched closely by the public, and that accidents would become matters of national concern.

The competition that preceded the line's opening had an important influence on the design of the locomotive. The directors of the Liverpool and Manchester had offered a prize for the best engine at a trial held at Rainhill in October 1829. Several entrants took part, including *Novelty*, *Sans Pareil*, and *Perseverance*, but the prize went to *Rocket*, a locomotive built by George and Robert Stephenson. *Rocket* used a multitubular boiler, which greatly increased the heating surface and allowed the engine to generate steam quickly, and it proved fast and reliable under the trial conditions. Its design became the template for locomotives that followed, and the multitubular boiler remained the basis of steam locomotive design for more than a century.

The Liverpool and Manchester also established practices that became standard. It ran trains to a timetable, with the purpose of allowing passengers and freight to be planned in advance. It used signals and rules to govern the movement of trains on the double track, and it began to develop a system of management in which different departments were responsible for locomotives, carriages, and the permanent way. These practices were not invented in a single moment, and some of them had antecedents in the older coal railways, but the Liverpool and Manchester brought them together on a scale that other companies would imitate. The railway as a managed system, rather than a collection of separate carriers, begins with this line.

## The Gauge Quarrel and the Railway Mania

By the late 1830s, the British railway had a problem that would take decades to solve. Engineers had settled on different track widths, which meant that trains from one line could not run on another. The most widely adopted gauge was the one used by George Stephenson's lines, which was four feet eight and a half inches, or about 1435 millimetres. This was roughly the width of the wagonways of the north-east, and it was convenient for the existing vehicles and horses. Isambard Kingdom Brunel, the engineer of the Great Western Railway, chose a much wider gauge of seven feet and a quarter inches, which he believed would allow higher speeds and greater stability. The Great Western opened in 1838 between London and Maidenhead, and it ran broad-gauge trains that were in many respects superior to the standard-gauge engines of the period.

The competing gauges created an expensive conflict. Where broad and narrow lines met, goods had to be transshipped from one wagon to another, and passengers had to change trains. The problem was not merely technical. Railway companies had strong commercial incentives to protect their own systems, and the gauge question became a matter of business rivalry as much as engineering judgement. Parliament eventually intervened. The Gauge Commission of the 1840s examined the evidence, and the Gauge Act of 1846 established the standard gauge as the norm for new lines, though the Great Western was permitted to keep its broad gauge on its existing system. The broad gauge survived for almost half a century before it was finally converted to standard gauge in 1892, and the last broad-gauge train ran in May of that year.

The gauge quarrel took place against a background of speculative frenzy. The period from about 1844 to 1847 is known as the Railway Mania, when investors poured money into new railway schemes, often without any clear understanding of their prospects. Hundreds of companies were promoted, many of them overlapping or duplicating routes, and the Parliamentary process was overwhelmed by the volume of bills. Shares were bought on the expectation that they would rise, and many of the schemes collapsed when the financial markets turned. The crash of 1847 caused widespread ruin, but it also left Britain with a network of railways that had been built largely at private expense, and the physical legacy of the mania was enormous. Much of the main-line system that still exists in Britain was laid down in these years.

The Railway Mania produced a wide range of social and cultural responses. Novelists and journalists wrote about the speculation, and cartoonists depicted the investors as credulous or greedy. Parliament responded with a series of Acts that regulated the new companies, and the Board of Trade was given a role in inspecting lines and approving their opening. The mania also produced the first generation of railway managers and professional engineers in large numbers, and the emerging profession became an important force in British industry. The railway was no longer a novelty. It was a major investment class and a central element of the economy.

## Continental Europe Takes the Rail

The railway crossed the English Channel in the sense of an idea within a few years of its first success, but the continental countries did not simply copy the British model. In each country, the railway was shaped by local politics, geography, and the financial systems available to fund it. In France, a line from Saint-Étienne to Lyon, opened in stages between 1832 and 1833, was one of the first in the country, and it was built partly to carry coal and partly to show the value of the new technology. The French government, which had grand plans for a national network, was often ambivalent about private railway companies, and it would later create a system of concessions in which private firms built and operated lines on terms set by the state.

Germany's first railway was the Ludwigsbahn, a line between Nuremberg and Fürth, which opened in December 1835. The line was short, and its locomotives were built by British engineers, but it demonstrated the appetite for railways in the German states, which were then fragmented into many separate kingdoms and principalities. Each state built its own lines, and the result was a patchwork of gauges, timetables, and tariffs that would take decades to rationalise. The German railway eventually became one of the most important in Europe, and its integration into a single national system came only after the unification of the country in 1871.

Belgium is often credited with the first major continental railway network, because the Belgian government chose to build lines directly as a state enterprise and to link the main cities of the country in a planned system. The first Belgian line, between Brussels and Mechelen, opened in 1835, and it was followed by a network that connected Antwerp, Ghent, and Liège. The state's direct involvement was unusual, and it gave Belgium an early and efficient system that served the industrial economy of the country. Belgian railways became a model for other states that wished to avoid the uncertainties of private speculation.

Russia built its first railway between Saint Petersburg and the imperial summer residence at Tsarskoye Selo, which opened in 1837. The line was a showpiece, and it was intended to demonstrate the modernity of the Russian state. The major Russian lines came later, and the great railway projects of the nineteenth century, including the links to Moscow and the southern ports, were carried out with a mixture of private and state capital. The Russian experience illustrates how railways could serve political as well as economic purposes, and how the choice of routes could be dictated by strategic and dynastic considerations.

Across Europe, the railway accelerated the movement of people and goods, and it changed patterns of settlement and commerce. Cities that were connected to the new network grew quickly, while those that were bypassed often declined. The railway also made possible new forms of national identity and administration, and governments came to see the network as an instrument of control. The timetable that the railway required imposed a new discipline on daily life, and the notion of standard local time gave way over time to a common railway time that was adopted by many towns.

## America Builds Across a Continent

The United States developed its own railway tradition, shaped by the vast distances of the continent and by the thin population of much of its territory. The Baltimore and Ohio Railroad, chartered in 1827, began operations in 1830 with horse-drawn cars, and it became the model for the large American railway companies of the following decades. The B&O was built to compete with the Erie Canal and with the Potomac canal projects, and it was intended to link the port of Baltimore with the Ohio River. Its early engines included Peter Cooper's *Tom Thumb*, a small experimental locomotive that made a demonstration run in 1830 and showed that steam power was practical on American track.

The South Carolina Canal and Rail Road Company introduced the steam locomotive *Best Friend of Charleston* in December 1830, and it became the first steam locomotive to haul a regular passenger train in the United States. The engine was a simple design and its boiler was a source of frequent trouble, and in June 1831 a fire caused by a leaking safety valve damaged the locomotive beyond repair. These early American railways were often built with light iron rails and simple locomotives, and their construction was adapted to the economic and physical conditions of the country. Many American lines were built to be cheap, and their engineers were willing to use methods that would not have been acceptable in Britain.

American railways expanded rapidly from the 1840s onward. The country had few existing roads and waterways in the regions being opened, and the railway offered a way to carry agricultural produce to markets and to bring settlers to the interior. Railroads were promoted by states, cities, and private investors, and they were often financed by land grants and bonds. The rivalry between cities for the position of the railway hub was intense, and many towns in the Midwest were founded or grew because they lay on a railroad. The railway created cities on the plains and the prairies, and its influence on the shape of American settlement was profound.

The most dramatic achievement of American railway building was the transcontinental line that linked the eastern and western sections of the country. Two companies, the Central Pacific building east from Sacramento and the Union Pacific building west from Omaha, laid track across the Rocky Mountains and the Sierra Nevada, using a combination of skilled and unskilled labour, including large numbers of Chinese and Irish workers. The lines met at Promontory Summit in Utah, and the last spike was driven on 10 May 1869. The completion of the transcontinental railroad was celebrated as a national achievement, and it altered the economics of the American West. The journey from the Atlantic to the Pacific, which had taken months by wagon or sea, could now be made in days.

American railways also developed distinctive technologies and institutions. George Pullman's sleeping car, first used in the 1860s, made long-distance travel more comfortable, and it created a company that would dominate the luxury rail market for decades. George Westinghouse's air brake, introduced in 1869, allowed a train's brakes to be applied simultaneously across all the wagons, a major improvement in safety. Eli Janney's automatic coupler, patented in 1873, replaced the dangerous practice of coupling wagons by hand, which had caused many deaths and injuries among brakemen. These innovations were the product of a continent-sized industry in which the economic incentives for safety and efficiency were strong.

The American railway also created the need for standard time. Before the late nineteenth century, each town kept its own local solar time, and the railways had to juggle many different clocks. On 18 November 1883, the major American railroads adopted a system of standard time zones, and local clocks were adjusted accordingly. The day was remembered as the day of two noons, because in some places the change required clocks to be set back or forward in the middle of the day. The railway had imposed a new order on time itself, and that order was later adopted by the wider society.

## Engineering the Impossible: Tunnels and Bridges

The railway's ability to conquer mountains and rivers depended on advances in civil engineering, and these advances were among the most dramatic of the nineteenth century. Early railways were built to follow the natural contours of the land as closely as possible, because cuttings, embankments, and bridges were expensive. As the network matured, engineers were called upon to cross larger obstacles, and the tunnel and the viaduct became the characteristic features of the mountain railway.

The Semmering Railway in Austria, completed in 1854, was one of the first great mountain lines in Europe. It crossed the Semmering Pass in the Alps south of Vienna, with a series of viaducts and tunnels that carried the line over steep gradients. The engineer Carl von Ghega designed the line, and his work was a landmark in the history of railway engineering. The viaducts were built of stone and were remarkably elegant, and the line demonstrated that a railway could be built through difficult terrain at a reasonable cost. Semmering is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and its engineering is still in service.

The great Alpine tunnels were another stage in this history. The Mont Cenis tunnel, also known as the Fréjus tunnel, was begun in 1857 and completed in 1871. It was roughly thirteen kilometres long and connected France and Italy beneath the Alps. Its construction was among the first to use mechanical rock drills powered by compressed air, which greatly increased the speed of excavation. The Gotthard tunnel, opened in 1882, was another great Alpine link, and it linked the German-speaking and Italian-speaking parts of Switzerland. Its construction was dangerous and expensive, and the tunnel's history was marked by accidents and labour disputes. These tunnels transformed the economic geography of Europe by making the Alps a route rather than a barrier.

In the United States, the Hoosac Tunnel in Massachusetts was one of the most notorious engineering projects of the nineteenth century. Begun in 1851 and completed in 1875, it was about seven and a half kilometres long, and its construction was long delayed by financial problems, flooding, and the difficulty of the rock. The tunnel was a costly project, and it became a symbol of the risks of public investment in large infrastructure. Its eventual completion showed what was possible with determination and new technology, but its history was also a warning about the financial dangers of ambitious public works.

Bridges were equally important. The Tay Bridge in Scotland, opened in 1878, was one of the longest bridges in the world when it was built, but it collapsed in a storm on 28 December 1879 as a train crossed it. The disaster killed everyone on board and prompted a close examination of design, materials, and wind loading. The Forth Bridge, designed by John Fowler and Benjamin Baker and opened in 1890, was built to a more conservative design and used steel on a massive scale. Its cantilever structure was among the most ambitious bridges of its time, and its appearance became an emblem of the railway age. The lessons of the Tay disaster influenced the design of later bridges, and the Forth was built with a deliberate attention to strength under load.

The Trans-Siberian Railway, begun in 1891 and completed in 1916, was an enormous engineering project that crossed thousands of kilometres of forest, steppe, and mountain. Its construction required the building of many bridges and tunnels, including the long bridge over the Ob River, and it was carried out under difficult conditions in a sparsely populated region. The railway was intended to tie the Russian Far East to the rest of the empire, and its strategic importance was obvious. The line became one of the great symbols of Russian industrial ambition, and it remains one of the longest railway lines in the world.

## Empires of Track: Asia, Africa, Australia

The railway was carried far beyond Europe and North America by the imperial and commercial expansion of the nineteenth century. In many cases the lines were built by colonial powers to serve their own interests, to move raw materials to the coast and to carry administrators and troops inland. The railway was therefore both an instrument of economic development and a tool of political control, and its legacy in the former colonies is still debated.

India was one of the largest railway projects of the nineteenth century, and it was built largely under British rule. The first line, between Bombay and Thane, opened in April 1853, and it was followed by a rapid expansion of the network. The Indian railways carried cotton, coal, and grain, and they also carried troops and officials. The system was built mostly by private companies under government guarantees, and it developed into one of the largest railway systems in the world. The network had a profound effect on Indian society, changing the movement of people and goods and creating new towns and industries. Its legacy is visible in the country's modern railway system, which remains one of the largest in the world.

Australia's railways began in the 1850s, and the first line in Victoria, between Melbourne and Port Melbourne, opened in 1854. The colonies built their own networks, and the lack of a common gauge became a problem in the late nineteenth century, as each colony chose a different track width. The consequences of this fragmentation persisted for decades, and the country did not achieve a national standard gauge until much later. Australian railways were essential to the opening of the interior, and they carried wool, wheat, and minerals to the coast. The railway also played a role in the nation's federation, as the need for coordination between the colonies became more urgent.

In Africa, railways were built to serve colonial economies, and their routes were often determined by the location of mines, ports, and administrative centres. The Cape Government Railways in South Africa, the lines that connected the mining districts of the Transvaal with the coast, were among the largest in the continent. The railway was central to the development of the mining industry, and it carried gold, diamonds, and coal. In other parts of Africa, railways were built with forced or poorly paid labour, and their construction often caused great suffering. The legacy of these lines is complicated, since they provided transport but were built to extract resources rather than to serve local populations.

In South America, railways were also built to export agricultural and mineral products to Europe and North America. The Argentine network, financed largely by British capital, became one of the most extensive in the region, and it played a central role in the country's rapid economic growth in the decades before the First World War. Chile and Brazil also developed substantial railway systems, and the railway was central to the expansion of mining and agriculture. Many of these lines were built by foreign companies, and their ownership later became a source of political conflict.

Across these regions, the railway was a powerful agent of change, but its impact was uneven. It could open remote areas to trade, but it could also tie them more tightly to distant markets and make them vulnerable to shifts in international prices. The railway's history in the non-European world is therefore a story of integration and dependency, and its legacy has been debated by historians and politicians alike.

## Standards, Signals and the Safety Problem

As railways grew in size and complexity, the need for standards and safety became more pressing. The early lines were often operated with little coordination, and accidents were common. Collisions, derailments, and boiler explosions killed many passengers and workers in the nineteenth century, and the public demanded that governments take action. The result was a gradual accumulation of rules, technologies, and institutions designed to make railways safer.

The signalling system was one of the most important developments in railway safety. Early railways relied on timetables and the judgement of drivers and guards, but as traffic increased, the need for a more systematic way of controlling train movements became clear. The block system, in which a line was divided into sections and only one train was allowed in each section at a time, was adopted in Britain in the 1840s and became a standard method of control. Signals were used to tell drivers whether a section was clear, and the signalmen who operated them became a distinct occupation. The electric telegraph, which was installed along many lines in the 1840s, allowed signalmen to communicate with one another and to coordinate movements over longer distances.

The introduction of continuous brakes was another major safety measure. Early trains were often braked by hand, with guards turning wheels on the wagons to slow them down. This system was slow and dangerous, and it made stopping a long train difficult. The air brake and the vacuum brake, which applied the brakes to every wagon simultaneously, transformed the safety of long trains. The adoption of the automatic coupler in the United States, after the Janney patent, also reduced the danger faced by brakemen, who had previously been injured or killed while coupling wagons by hand.

Standardisation of technical practices was another part of this story. Railways needed common rules for the design of locomotives, the spacing of wheels, the composition of trains, and the construction of tracks. The organisations that developed these standards, such as the Railway Clearing House in Britain, which managed the sharing of revenue between companies, were essential to the functioning of the network. The development of common standards allowed trains to pass from one company's territory to another and made the railway a truly national system.

Accidents remained a central concern throughout this period. Investigations after major disasters led to new regulations, and the reports of inspectors were an important source of public information. The most famous British inquiry, into the Abermule collision of 1921 and similar accidents, led to further improvements in signalling and in the design of safe operating practices. The railway's safety record improved greatly over the twentieth century, but the problem of coordinating large numbers of trains over complex networks has never been entirely solved, and it continues to shape the design of modern signalling systems.

## The Age of Electricity

The application of electricity to railways began almost as soon as electric motors became practical. Werner von Siemens, the German engineer and industrialist, built an electric railway at the Berlin Trade Exhibition in 1879, and in the following year he opened a line at Lichterfelde near Berlin that carried passengers. The early electric trains were small and ran on low voltages with a third rail or an overhead wire, and they demonstrated the potential of electric traction for urban and suburban services. The electric tram and the urban railway were the first beneficiaries of the new technology.

Electric traction offered several advantages over steam. It produced no smoke and no ash, which was an important consideration in tunnels and cities. It accelerated more quickly than steam locomotives and could stop more rapidly, and it could be easily controlled from a central point. It also allowed the power to be generated in a single place rather than carried on each locomotive. The disadvantage was the cost of building the infrastructure, including power stations, substations, and overhead wires, and this cost meant that electrification was usually limited to lines with heavy traffic.

Several important electric systems were built in the early twentieth century. The Baltimore and Ohio Railroad electrified its tunnel through the city of Baltimore in 1895, using a direct-current system, and this project became an early demonstration of electric traction for heavy freight and passenger service. In Italy, the Valtellina line, opened in 1902, used three-phase alternating current, which was a complex system that required two overhead wires and was eventually superseded by simpler designs. The choice between direct current and alternating current was one of the central technical debates of early electrification, and the eventual dominance of alternating current in the mainline system was a product of its advantages in transmission over long distances.

The electrification of suburban railways was a major achievement in Britain, the United States, and continental Europe in the early twentieth century. The London Underground, which had begun with steam and was electrified in the 1900s, became a model for urban rapid transit. Electric lines around large cities allowed frequent services and rapid acceleration, and they helped to shape the growth of suburbs. The electric interurban railways of the United States, which connected towns and cities across the country, were a distinctive development that flourished for a few decades before the rise of the automobile reduced their importance.

Electrification of main lines progressed more slowly, partly because of the cost and partly because of the availability of alternative technologies. In many countries, electrification was limited to particular corridors, and steam continued to dominate much of the network until the middle of the twentieth century. The electric locomotive, with its ability to produce high power and smooth acceleration, became the preferred motive power for heavy traffic in mountainous regions and in areas with abundant hydroelectric power, such as Switzerland and Italy. The Swiss railways, which had little coal and abundant water power, were among the first to make extensive use of electric traction on their mainlines.

## Diesel, Streamlining and the Speed Record

The diesel engine, invented by Rudolf Diesel in the 1890s, offered a different route to the replacement of steam. Diesel engines were efficient, and they could run on oil rather than coal, which made them attractive in places where fuel was scarce or expensive. The first diesel locomotives were built in the early twentieth century, and a Swiss prototype of 1912 from the Winterthur works is often cited as an early example of the type. These locomotives were initially heavy and unreliable, and the mechanical transmissions of the period were not well suited to traction. The diesel locomotive took decades to mature.

The breakthrough came with the diesel-electric locomotive, in which a diesel engine drove an electric generator that supplied current to traction motors on the axles. This arrangement solved many of the problems of mechanical transmission. It gave smooth control over the power delivered to the wheels, it allowed several locomotives to be coupled together and controlled from one cab, and it reduced the maintenance costs compared with steam. In the United States, the Electro-Motive Division of General Motors, and the later companies that developed the diesel-electric locomotive, produced machines that rapidly displaced steam on many lines after the Second World War. The Electro-Motive F-series locomotives of the late 1930s and 1940s became iconic, and they showed that diesel traction could be reliable, economic, and powerful.

Streamlining was a major design trend of the 1930s. Railway companies commissioned streamlined trains to attract passengers and to demonstrate the modernity of the railway. The Burlington Zephyr, a lightweight diesel-electric train built by the Budd Company and introduced in 1934, was one of the most famous examples. It made a record-breaking run from Denver to Chicago in 1934, averaging a speed that impressed contemporaries and attracted enormous publicity. Streamlined trains were also built in Germany, Britain, and elsewhere, and they reflected the era's enthusiasm for speed, design, and technological progress.

The speed record for steam locomotives was set in Britain in 1938, when the LNER Class A4 locomotive *Mallard* reached 126 miles per hour, or about 203 kilometres per hour, on a descent near Stoke Bank in Lincolnshire. The record was set on 3 July 1938 and has never been beaten by a steam locomotive. The achievement was remarkable because steam locomotives were not designed for the highest speeds, and the engine's performance depended on careful engineering and the skill of its crew. *Mallard* remains a symbol of the steam age's engineering peak, and its record shows how far the steam locomotive could be pushed.

The period between the wars also saw the development of new forms of rail traction in Germany and elsewhere. The Fliegender Hamburger, a diesel railcar introduced in 1933, was one of the first high-speed diesel trains in regular service, and it demonstrated that lightweight diesel units could replace steam on fast regional services. The enthusiasm for speed and modernity in these years prepared the ground for later developments, and it showed the railway's ability to adapt to new technologies.

## Mid-century Decline and Nationalisation

After the Second World War, the railway faced a period of profound change. Road transport, which had been growing for decades, expanded rapidly with the spread of cars and lorries, and the railway lost passengers and freight to competitors. In many countries, the railway's finances deteriorated, and governments became more involved in its management. The post-war period was marked by nationalisation, rationalisation, and in many cases, the closure of lines that were judged to be uneconomic.

In Britain, the railways were nationalised in 1948 under the British Transport Commission, and the newly created British Railways inherited a network that had been damaged by the war and by decades of underinvestment. The new system was large and complex, and its management struggled to modernise it. In 1963, the Beeching Report recommended the closure of many lines and stations that were judged to be unprofitable, and the subsequent programme of closures removed thousands of miles of track and hundreds of stations from the network. The Beeching cuts became one of the most controversial episodes in British transport history, and they shaped the public memory of the railway for decades.

The United States experienced a different form of decline. Passenger traffic fell sharply after the war, as Americans turned to cars and aeroplanes. The Penn Central Transportation Company, formed in 1968 from the merger of two major eastern railroads, went bankrupt in 1970, and the collapse of the company led to government intervention. The National Railroad Passenger Corporation, known as Amtrak, was created in 1971 to take over most of the country's intercity passenger services, and the Consolidated Rail Corporation, or Conrail, was formed in 1976 to take over the bankrupt freight lines of the north-east. The Staggers Rail Act of 1980 deregulated freight rates and allowed railroads to compete more freely, and this change helped the freight railroads to recover financially.

The deregulation of freight in the United States produced a remarkable revival. Freight railroads became more efficient, and they invested in heavy haul, containerisation, and improved locomotives. The volume of freight carried by American railways grew substantially, and the railroads became profitable again in the following decades. Passenger traffic, by contrast, remained limited, and Amtrak continued to depend on public subsidy. The American experience showed that the freight railway and the passenger railway could have very different economic prospects, and that the policy environment could determine which of them flourished.

In much of continental Europe, railways remained more central to national transport, and state railway companies continued to operate most services. The French national railway, the SNCF, was created in 1938 from the merger of several companies, and it became a symbol of the state's commitment to rail transport. The German Federal Railway and the Swiss Federal Railways continued to be major public enterprises, and their networks remained substantial. These systems were less affected by the decline of the post-war years, partly because of higher population densities and partly because of strong public support for rail.

Japan's railways, which had been built largely by the state, were reorganised after the Second World War. The Japanese National Railways was a large public enterprise that struggled with debt and labour problems in the 1970s and 1980s. Its eventual privatisation in 1987 created several regional companies, which operated the passenger network with greater commercial freedom. The Japanese experience illustrated the difficulties of managing a large public railway in a changing economy, and it also set the stage for the expansion of high-speed rail in the following decades.

## The Shinkansen and the Birth of High-Speed Rail

The Tokaido Shinkansen, which opened on 1 October 1964, is generally regarded as the first high-speed railway in the modern sense. It connected Tokyo with Shin-Osaka, a distance of about 515 kilometres, and it was built as a dedicated line with standard gauge track, grade separation, and new rolling stock designed for high speed. The line was built in a remarkably short time, and it was opened in time for the Tokyo Olympic Games of that year. Its trains, the first Shinkansen series, were designed to run at up to 210 kilometres per hour, a speed that was then much faster than any other passenger service in the world.

The Shinkansen's success depended on several factors. The line was built on a new alignment, with gentle curves and wide radii, which allowed high speeds. The tracks were laid with heavy rails and continuous welded sections, which reduced vibration and noise. The trains were designed with streamlined noses and aerodynamic features, and they had powerful traction systems that allowed rapid acceleration. The signalling was automatic, and the line was operated with a high degree of coordination. The result was a service that was frequent, punctual, and remarkably safe, and it transformed travel between the major cities of Japan.

The Shinkansen was not simply a technical achievement. It was part of a broader national project of economic recovery and modernisation, and it symbolised Japan's return to the international stage after the war. Its success attracted attention from engineers and governments around the world, and it demonstrated that high-speed rail could be commercially viable. Over the following decades, the Shinkansen network expanded across Japan, and new lines were built to the north and south of the original route. The system became famous for its punctuality, cleanliness, and safety, and it has carried billions of passengers without a passenger fatality from derailment or collision in its history.

The early Shinkansen also demonstrated the importance of dedicated infrastructure. Trains running at high speed on shared track were difficult to manage, and separate lines were needed to allow high speeds and frequent services. This principle has guided most high-speed rail development since, though some countries have built high-speed trains that run on existing lines at lower speeds. The Shinkansen's design also showed the importance of reliability, since a high-speed service depends on a high degree of precision in every aspect of operation.

## France, Germany and the European Network

France was the second country to develop high-speed rail on a large scale, and its Train à Grande Vitesse, or TGV, became one of the most successful high-speed systems in the world. The first commercial TGV line, between Paris and Lyon, opened on 27 September 1981, and it reduced the journey time between the two cities to about two hours. The line was built as a dedicated high-speed route, and the trains were designed to run at up to 270 kilometres per hour, a speed that was then unmatched in regular service in Europe. The success of the Paris–Lyon line encouraged the French government to plan a national network of high-speed lines radiating from Paris.

The TGV's technical development was closely watched by other countries. The trains used articulated carriages, with a single bogie shared between adjacent carriages, which reduced weight and improved stability at high speed. The power cars were distributed along the train, and the traction system allowed the trains to be operated from both ends. The TGV also established records for speed on conventional rail, and in 1990 a TGV set a world speed record for conventional wheel-on-rail trains of 515.3 kilometres per hour, a mark that stood for many years. Later, in 2007, a specially prepared TGV reached 574.8 kilometres per hour, which remains the speed record for conventional railway trains.

Germany developed its own high-speed system, the Intercity-Express, or ICE, which entered service in 1991. The ICE was designed to run at high speeds on newly built lines and on upgraded routes. Germany's approach was more varied than France's, since its network was older and more complex, and the ICE was designed to operate on both dedicated high-speed tracks and conventional lines. The ICE's design also reflected the German emphasis on engineering rigour and on the integration of high-speed services into a wider network of regional and intercity trains. The German system has been criticised for its cost and its complexity, but it has also been credited with raising the standards of rail travel in the country.

Spain built one of the largest high-speed networks in Europe, beginning with the line from Madrid to Seville, which opened in 1992 in time for the Seville Expo. The Spanish network, which uses a broad gauge that differs from the standard gauge of most of Europe, has expanded rapidly since then and now covers many of the country's major cities. The Spanish case illustrates how high-speed rail can be used as an instrument of regional development, and how it can attract passengers from air and road. Italy, which built its first high-speed line between Rome and Florence in the early 1990s, has also developed a substantial network of fast trains.

The European high-speed network has also been shaped by the European Union's policies on interoperability and competition. The European Rail Traffic Management System, known as ERTMS, is a common signalling and train control system designed to allow trains to cross borders without changing equipment. The Channel Tunnel, opened in 1994, linked Britain and France by rail, and the Eurostar service that runs through it has become an important part of the European network. The Channel Tunnel is about fifty kilometres long, of which roughly thirty-eight kilometres lie under the sea, and it was one of the largest infrastructure projects of its time.

The high-speed network in Europe has changed patterns of travel and commerce. Cities that were once separated by many hours of travel are now connected by trains of two or three hours, and the air routes between them have declined in many cases. The high-speed train has become a competitor to the aeroplane on routes of several hundred kilometres, and its environmental advantages have made it attractive to policymakers concerned with carbon emissions. The debate about the cost of high-speed rail has been intense, and it continues to shape decisions about new lines and their financing.

## China, Scale and the Modern Race

China's high-speed railway is the largest in the world by a wide margin, and its growth over the past two decades has been extraordinary. The first Chinese high-speed lines were built in the late 2000s, and the country quickly developed a network that by the mid-2020s extended over more than forty thousand kilometres. The network connects most of the major cities of the country, and its trains run at speeds of up to 350 kilometres per hour on many routes. The rapid expansion was driven by government investment, by the desire to link regions, and by the aim of building an industrial base for high-speed rolling stock.

The Chinese approach to high-speed rail combined the import of foreign technology with domestic development. Early trains were built under licence from foreign manufacturers, and their designs were adapted to Chinese conditions. Over time, Chinese companies developed their own trains, and they began to export them to other countries. The speed of this development was unusual, and it reflected a concentrated industrial policy and a willingness to invest heavily in infrastructure. The Beijing to Tianjin line, which opened in 2008 before the Beijing Olympics, was one of the first Chinese lines designed for high speed, and it was followed by a rapid expansion across the country.

The Chinese network has transformed travel within the country. Journeys that once took a day or more can now be made in a few hours, and the high-speed train has become the preferred means of travel for many business and leisure passengers. The system has also raised concerns about debt, cost, and the financial sustainability of some lines, particularly in less populated regions. Critics have argued that some lines were built with insufficient demand, and that the financing of the network has created risks for the government and the banking system. The Chinese experience has therefore prompted a wider debate about the economics of high-speed rail in general.

China's rise as a builder of high-speed rail has also had international significance. Chinese companies have bid for high-speed projects in other countries, and the Chinese government has promoted its railway technology as part of its broader economic and diplomatic strategy. Projects in Southeast Asia, Africa, and Latin America have been developed with Chinese participation, and the competition with Japanese and European firms has become part of the global market for rail technology. The development of high-speed rail has thus become a question of industrial and geopolitical strategy as well as of transport policy.

Other countries in Asia have also built high-speed networks. South Korea's KTX, which began service in 2004, runs on dedicated lines between Seoul and the southern cities, and it has become an important part of the country's transport system. Taiwan's high-speed railway, which opened in 2007, runs along the western coast of the island and links Taipei with Kaohsiung. These systems show that high-speed rail can be adapted to a wide range of geographical and economic conditions, and that the technology has spread far beyond its original home in Japan.

## Maglev and the Limits of Speed

Magnetic levitation, or maglev, offers a different approach to very high speeds. Instead of running on wheels, maglev trains are supported and propelled by magnetic forces, which eliminates the friction of the wheel on the rail and allows speeds that are difficult to achieve with conventional trains. Two main types of maglev have been developed: electromagnetic suspension, in which electromagnets on the train are attracted to a steel rail, and electrodynamic suspension, in which superconducting magnets on the train induce currents in conducting coils on the guideway.

The German Transrapid system was one of the first maglev technologies to reach commercial service. The Shanghai Maglev Train, which uses the Transrapid design, began carrying passengers in 2004 on a route of about thirty kilometres between Pudong International Airport and the outskirts of the city. The line can reach speeds of more than 400 kilometres per hour, and it has become a symbol of Chinese engineering ambition. However, its high cost and its limited route have meant that it has not been widely copied, and the Chinese government has not extended the system to other cities.

The Japanese SCMaglev, a superconducting electrodynamic system, has been developed over several decades, and it has achieved remarkable speeds in test conditions. In December 2015, a test train on a Japanese test track reached 603 kilometres per hour, a world record for rail vehicles. The Japanese government has supported the construction of a line between Tokyo and Nagoya, and it has also planned an extension to Osaka. The project has faced delays and cost overruns, and its completion has been pushed back several times. The SCMaglev's future depends on the outcome of these projects and on the costs of construction and operation.

Maglev illustrates the limits of speed as a design goal. Very high speeds bring problems of energy consumption, noise, and the need for specialised infrastructure. A maglev line requires a dedicated guideway, and its construction is expensive. For many routes, the marginal gain in speed does not justify the additional cost, and conventional high-speed rail offers a more practical solution. The challenge for maglev is to find routes where its speed advantage is sufficient to justify its price, and that remains an open question.

The debate over maglev also reflects a broader tension in transport policy between the desire for technological novelty and the need for economic practicality. The history of the railway shows that many innovations have been overtaken by simpler and cheaper alternatives, and that the most successful systems are often those that combine incremental improvement with reliable service. Maglev may yet find its niche, but its history so far suggests that the wheel on the rail has remained a remarkably durable solution.

## Freight, Cost and the Question Ahead

Freight remains one of the most important functions of the railway, and it has been a major factor in the economic performance of many countries. Railways carry bulk commodities such as coal, ore, grain, and chemicals over long distances, and they do so with lower energy consumption and emissions per tonne than road transport. The efficiency of rail freight depends on the scale of the traffic, the quality of the infrastructure, and the organisation of the service. Container traffic, which has grown rapidly since the 1960s, has been one of the most important developments in modern rail freight, and it has linked ports and inland terminals in complex networks.

The economic case for railways has always depended on the balance between fixed costs and operating costs. Railways require heavy investment in track, signalling, stations, and rolling stock, and they need high traffic volumes to repay that investment. Where traffic is dense, the railway can be extremely efficient, and where it is sparse, the cost per passenger or tonne can be very high. This is the central problem that every railway system must confront, and it explains many of the policy decisions that have shaped the railway's history, from the closures of the Beeching era to the subsidies of modern passenger services.

The environmental argument for rail has grown stronger in recent decades. Concern about carbon emissions has made the railway attractive to policymakers who wish to reduce the impact of transport, and electrified railways powered by low-carbon electricity can offer a much cleaner alternative to road and air travel. The high-speed train has been promoted as a substitute for short-haul flights, and some countries have introduced policies to encourage this shift. However, the extent to which rail can replace other modes depends on the availability of routes, the quality of service, and the willingness of passengers to change their habits.

The technological future of the railway is uncertain. Autonomous operation, digital signalling, and new forms of traction may change the way trains are run and maintained. The European Train Control System and similar digital systems are intended to improve capacity and safety, and they may allow more trains to run on existing lines. New materials and designs may reduce the weight of trains and the wear on tracks, and advances in energy storage may allow trains to run on routes without continuous overhead wires. The railway has repeatedly reinvented itself, and there is every reason to expect that it will continue to do so.

The railway's history suggests that its future will depend less on any single invention than on the wider choices that societies make about how to move people and goods. The wooden wagonways of the sixteenth century were a response to the economics of mining, and the high-speed lines of today are a response to the economics of dense urban and intercity travel. The railway has always been shaped by the needs of its time and by the political and financial structures that govern it. Its story is one of continuous adaptation, and the question of its future is the question of which needs will matter most in the decades ahead.
